## The question

[Equation of tangent to the curve](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4749591/equation-of-tangent-to-the-curve), asked by [user3.14](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1201323/user3-14) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-08-08; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> The equation of the curve is:
>
> $$x=\frac{\left(y-2\right)^{2}}{y}$$
>
> The tangent to the curve is passing through the origin. Find the equation of the tangent.
>
> My solution:
>
> $xy=(y-2)^2$
>
> ⇒ $x=\frac{(y-2)^2}{y}$ 
>
> Now, differentiating both sides with respect to y, we get,
>
> $\frac{dx}{dy}= \frac{(y-2)(y+2)}{y^2}$
>
> Therefore, $\frac{dy}{dx}= \frac{y^2}{(y-2)(y+2)}$
>
> The equation of tangent is given by, $y-y_1$= $\frac{dy}{dx}(x-x_1)$.
>
> Since, tangent passes through origin, so at $(0,0)$, $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$
>
> Thus, the equation of tangent is: $y-0= 0(x-0)$
>
> ⇒ $y$=$0$  (i.e X-axis)
>
> My confusion: Tangent exists at a point on the curve, but looking at the graph of $xy=(y-2)^{2}$, we can see that X-axis is the asymptote, so how can the tangent be $y=0$ i.e. X-axis when curve doesn't even touch it?
>
> Following is the graph of $x=\frac{\left(y-2\right)^{2}}{y}$
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
>   [q-1]: YVAus.gif
:::

> The equation of tangent is given by, $y-y_1$= $\frac{dy}{dx}(x-x_1)$.
>
> Since, tangent passes through origin, so at $(0,0)$, $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$

I think your mistake is here. Since the tangent line to the curve at $(x_1,y_1)$ passes through the origin, we know $y-y_1 = \frac{dy}{dx}(x_1,y_1)(x-x_1)$ is satisfied by $x=0$ and $y=0$. That tells you something about $(x_1,y_1)$: namely, that $\frac{dy}{dx}(x_1,y_1) = \frac{y_1}{x_1}$. So you want to find solutions to $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x}$. 

Another possibility is a vertical tangent line. If this vertical tangent line passes through the origin, it must be the $y$-axis. So look for points $(0,y_1)$ on the curve with $\frac{dx}{dy}(0,y_1) = 0$.
